example: Atoms are the basic building blocks of materials.
The nucleus contains almost all of an atom's mass.
The number of protons determines the atomic number of an element.
Isotopes of the same element have different numbers of neutrons.
Electron transfer and sharing determine how atoms form chemical bonds.
Valence electrons largely control the bonding behavior of an atom.
Electron configuration helps explain periodic trends in chemical behavior.
The principal quantum number identifies the main energy level of an electron.
The Pauli exclusion principle prevents two electrons in one atom from sharing all four quantum numbers.
Hund's rule predicts that degenerate orbitals fill singly before electron pairing occurs.
The periodic table groups elements with similar valence-electron configurations and properties.
Silver has an atomic number of 47 because each silver atom contains 47 protons.
Atomic radius affects interatomic spacing and many trends in crystal structure.
Interatomic bonding strongly influences stiffness, melting point, and electrical behavior.
Metallic, ionic, and covalent bonds are the main types of primary bonds in materials.
Secondary bonds are weaker than primary bonds but can strongly affect polymers and molecular solids.
Metallic bonding helps explain the good electrical conductivity of metals.
An ionic bond is formed by electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions.
Covalent bonds have strong directionality in many materials.
Van der Waals forces help hold weakly bonded molecular layers together.
Hydrogen bonding can raise the strength and thermal stability of some polymers.
A high bond energy usually corresponds to a strong bond and a high melting temperature.
A large electronegativity difference between two atoms favors ionic bonding.
Polarization describes the displacement of positive and negative charge centers in an electric field.
A permanent dipole forms when positive and negative charge centers do not coincide.

A crystal has a long-range ordered atomic structure.
A crystalline metal produces sharp diffraction peaks because its atoms repeat periodically over long distances.
Metallic glass is an amorphous material because it lacks long-range periodic atomic order.
Long-range order allows a crystal lattice to repeat over many unit cells.
A glass can retain short-range order among neighboring atoms even without a periodic lattice.
A lattice represents the periodic positions that are repeated throughout a crystal.
A space lattice extends the periodic arrangement of lattice points in three dimensions.
Every lattice point in an ideal lattice has an equivalent surrounding environment.
Placing the same atomic basis on every lattice point generates a crystal structure.
The crystal structure of FCC copper can be described by an FCC lattice and a one-atom basis.
A unit cell is the basic repeating unit of a crystal.
A primitive cell contains the minimum volume needed to reproduce the entire lattice by translation.
The lattice parameter of FCC silver changes slightly with temperature because of thermal expansion.
The fourteen Bravais lattices classify all possible three-dimensional translational lattices.
Cubic, tetragonal, and hexagonal are three of the seven crystal systems.
In a cubic crystal, the [110] crystallographic direction runs along a face diagonal.
Direction indices such as [111] specify a crystallographic direction using the smallest integer components.
A crystallographic plane cuts the lattice at positions determined by its orientation and spacing.
Miller indices (111) identify one family member of close-packed planes in an FCC crystal.
The family of directions ⟨110⟩ contains symmetry-equivalent directions in a cubic crystal.
The family of planes {111} contains symmetry-equivalent planes in an FCC crystal.
A stereographic projection can display the angular relationship between crystal planes on a two-dimensional chart.
Crystal symmetry determines which directions and planes are equivalent under symmetry operations.
Each atom in an ideal FCC structure has a coordination number of 12.
FCC and HCP structures have an atomic packing factor of 0.74, while BCC is about 0.68.
The {111} planes are the close-packed planes in an FCC crystal.
The ⟨110⟩ directions are close-packed directions in FCC metals.
Silver has a face-centered cubic structure in its bulk form.
Ferrite has a body-centered cubic structure.
HCP and FCC are both close-packed structures.
FCC and HCP differ mainly in their stacking sequences.
ABC stacking of close-packed atomic layers produces the FCC structure.
AB stacking of close-packed layers produces the ideal HCP structure.
A small interstitial atom can occupy a tetrahedral site surrounded by four host atoms.
An octahedral site is surrounded by six nearest host atoms.
Carbon occupies interstitial sites in iron because carbon atoms are much smaller than iron atoms.
Polymorphism allows the same compound to crystallize in more than one crystal structure.
Iron exhibits allotropy because its stable crystal structure changes from BCC to FCC with temperature.
A solid solution contains solute atoms dissolved in a solvent lattice.
In a substitutional solid solution, solute atoms replace host atoms on normal lattice sites.
Carbon in ferrite forms an interstitial solid solution by occupying small sites in the BCC iron lattice.
An intermediate phase can appear between terminal solid solutions in a binary alloy system.
Intermetallic compounds often have ordered structures and properties distinct from their constituent metals.
In an ordered solid solution, different atomic species preferentially occupy specific lattice sites.
In a disordered solid solution, solute and solvent atoms occupy equivalent lattice sites statistically at random.
Sodium chloride is an ionic crystal held together mainly by electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions.
Diamond is a covalent crystal in which each carbon atom forms strong directional covalent bonds.
Polyethylene can form polymer crystals when segments of its long chains pack into ordered regions.
